description: Heart structure, the pathway of blood and how the cardiovascular system responds to physical activity.
content_html:
The Heart and Blood: Delivering Oxygen to Working Muscles

The cardiovascular system is the body’s transport network. It delivers oxygen and nutrients to every working cell and removes waste products including carbon dioxide and heat. During exercise, the demand for oxygen in the muscles multiplies, and the cardiovascular system responds with a series of rapid adjustments to maintain performance. Understanding these structures and responses is central to this topic.

Functions of the Cardiovascular System

The cardiovascular system has four key functions in physical activity. First, transport of oxygen: red blood cells carry oxygen from the lungs to working muscles, enabling aerobic energy production. Second, transport of carbon dioxide: blood carries CO&sub2; away from muscles back to the lungs for exhalation. Third, transport of nutrients: glucose and fatty acids travel in the plasma to fuel muscle contractions. Fourth, regulation of body temperature: blood carries heat from working muscles to the skin surface, where it can be dissipated through sweating and radiation.

Additionally, blood contributes to clotting of open wounds via platelets — protecting athletes from blood loss after contact injuries — and to immune defence via white blood cells.

Structure of the Heart

The heart is a double pump, divided into left and right sides by the septum. Each side has an upper chamber (an atrium) and a lower chamber (a ventricle). The right side deals with deoxygenated blood; the left side deals with oxygenated blood.

Blood flows through the heart in a precise sequence. Deoxygenated blood from the body enters the right atrium via the vena cava (the large vein returning blood from the upper and lower body). It passes through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle. From there it is pumped out through the pulmonary artery to the lungs to pick up oxygen. Oxygenated blood returns from the lungs via the pulmonary vein into the left atrium. It passes through the bicuspid (mitral) valve into the left ventricle, which pumps it out through the aorta to the rest of the body.

The semi-lunar valves sit at the exits of both ventricles — one at the base of the pulmonary artery (pulmonary semi-lunar valve) and one at the base of the aorta (aortic semi-lunar valve). Their job is to prevent blood flowing back into the ventricles after each contraction. The “lub-dub” sound of the heartbeat is the sound of these valves — and the atrioventricular valves (tricuspid and bicuspid) — snapping shut.

Key Fact

Blood pathway through the heart: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid valve → left ventricle → aorta → body.

Blood Vessels: Arteries, Capillaries and Veins

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure. Their thick, muscular and elastic walls withstand and smooth out the surges of pressure produced by each heartbeat. The aorta is the largest artery, branching into progressively smaller arteries as it distributes blood to all regions of the body.

Capillaries are the smallest vessels, with walls only one cell thick. This ultra-thin wall allows oxygen, glucose and carbon dioxide to diffuse freely between the blood and the muscle fibres. A dense network of capillaries surrounds every active muscle fibre, and endurance training increases the density of this network — one of the key long-term adaptations covered in Lesson 9.

Veins return blood to the heart under low pressure. Their walls are thinner than arteries because the pressure is much lower. Veins contain valves that prevent blood from flowing backwards (particularly important in the legs where blood must travel upward against gravity).

Cardiac Output, Stroke Volume and Heart Rate

Cardiac output (Q) is the total amount of blood pumped by the heart per minute. It is calculated by the formula:

$$Q = \text{stroke volume} \times \text{heart rate}$$

Stroke volume (SV) is the amount of blood pumped out with each beat. At rest a typical adult has a stroke volume of around 70 ml. Heart rate (HR) at rest is typically 60–80 bpm. So resting cardiac output is approximately 70 × 70 = 4,900 ml/min (roughly 5 litres per minute).

During maximal exercise, heart rate can reach 200 bpm and stroke volume can increase to 110–130 ml in a fit person, giving a cardiac output of over 20 litres per minute — a four-fold increase. This increased delivery of oxygenated blood to muscles is the central cardiovascular response to exercise.

Key Fact

Cardiac output (Q) = stroke volume (SV) × heart rate (HR). At rest: ~70 ml × 70 bpm = ~4,900 ml/min. During maximal exercise: cardiac output can exceed 20,000 ml/min (20 L/min) as both SV and HR increase.

Vascular shunting is the process by which blood is redirected during exercise. At rest, organs such as the gut, liver and kidneys receive a large proportion of cardiac output. During intense exercise, the arterioles supplying these organs vasoconstrict (their smooth muscle contracts, narrowing the vessel), while the arterioles supplying the working muscles vasodilate (relax and widen), directing a much greater fraction of cardiac output to the muscles that need it. This redistribution can shift up to 80% of cardiac output to working muscles during maximal exercise, compared with around 15–20% at rest.

Blood is a mixture of cells and fluid. Red blood cells (erythrocytes) contain haemoglobin, which binds oxygen in the lungs and releases it in the muscles. They have no nucleus, maximising their oxygen-carrying capacity. White blood cells (leucocytes) form part of the immune system, destroying pathogens. Platelets (thrombocytes) trigger blood clotting when a vessel is damaged. Plasma is the fluid component (about 55% of blood volume) that transports cells, dissolved gases, nutrients, hormones and waste products. Plasma also distributes heat generated by working muscles to the skin for cooling.
exam_tip_html: Calculation questions on cardiac output follow a simple two-step pattern: (1) write the formula, Q = SV × HR; (2) substitute the values; (3) state the answer with units (ml/min or L/min). Always include units — the mark scheme requires them. On Explain questions about exercise responses, use the ‘what changes → why → so that’ chain: ‘heart rate increases (what) because the sympathetic nervous system sends signals to the sinoatrial node (why), so that more oxygen-rich blood reaches working muscles (so that).’ On valve questions, remember: tricuspid is on the right, bicuspid on the left. A useful memory aid: bicuspid has two flaps and is on the left side — two letters in ‘left’, two flaps.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The heart is a four-chambered double pump: right side moves deoxygenated blood to the lungs; left side moves oxygenated blood to the body. Blood flows through in the sequence: vena cava → right atrium → tricuspid → right ventricle → pulmonary artery → lungs → pulmonary vein → left atrium → bicuspid → left ventricle → aorta.
  • Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate. At rest, around 5 L/min; during maximal exercise, over 20 L/min — driven by increases in both stroke volume and heart rate.
  • Arteries carry blood away from the heart under high pressure; capillaries are the site of gas and nutrient exchange; veins return blood to the heart under low pressure. Vascular shunting redirects blood to working muscles during exercise.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of the bicuspid valve?
A) It separates the left and right sides of the heart
B) It prevents backflow between the right atrium and right ventricle
C) It prevents backflow between the left atrium and left ventricle
D) It controls blood flow from the left ventricle into the aorta
practice_questions.marks: C) It prevents backflow between the left atrium and left ventricle [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old athlete has a resting heart rate of 65 bpm and a stroke volume of 75 ml. Calculate her resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working: Q = 75 ml × 65 bpm. 1 mark for correct answer with units: 4,875 ml/min (accept 4.875 L/min). No mark if units are missing or if formula is not shown.

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of vascular shunting during exercise and explain its importance for performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for what vascular shunting is: redistribution of blood flow from non-essential organs to working muscles during exercise. 1 mark for the mechanism: arterioles supplying non-essential organs vasoconstrict; arterioles in working muscles vasodilate. 1 mark for the performance importance: ensures working muscles receive a much greater proportion of the increased cardiac output, maximising oxygen delivery and waste removal.

practice_questions.text:
The table below shows heart rate and stroke volume data for a recreational runner at rest and at three exercise intensities.

Condition        | Heart rate (bpm) | Stroke volume (ml)
Rest             | 70               | 70
Light exercise   | 100              | 85
Moderate exercise| 145              | 110
Maximal exercise | 190              | 120

Calculate the cardiac output at maximal exercise and compare it to resting cardiac output.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for maximal cardiac output calculation: 190 × 120 = 22,800 ml/min (22.8 L/min). 1 mark for comparison with resting: resting Q = 70 × 70 = 4,900 ml/min; maximal is approximately 4.7 times greater / an increase of about 17,900 ml/min. Accept correct figures based on the data given.

practice_questions.text: Explain the sequence of blood flow through the heart during one cardiac cycle, naming all chambers, valves and major vessels.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks for correctly sequencing: deoxygenated blood enters right atrium via vena cava (1); passes through tricuspid valve into right ventricle, then out via pulmonary artery to lungs (1); oxygenated blood returns via pulmonary vein to left atrium, passes through bicuspid valve into left ventricle, exits through aorta to the body (1). Deduct no marks if semi-lunar valves are not mentioned, but credit if included.

practice_questions.text: A school swimming coach claims that cardiovascular fitness is the most important component of fitness for a 400 m swimmer. Assess this claim, referring to the structure and function of the cardiovascular system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Strong case for cardiovascular fitness: a 400 m swim lasts approximately 4 minutes at high intensity, requiring sustained aerobic energy; the cardiovascular system must maintain high cardiac output (high SV and HR), effective vascular shunting to arm and leg muscles, and efficient gas exchange via dense capillary networks. Counterargument: muscular endurance and technique efficiency also matter. Structured judgement: e.g. 'cardiovascular fitness is the primary limiting factor at 400 m — the aerobic system dominates, and a well-trained heart increases stroke volume and therefore sustained cardiac output — but it is not the only factor.' Technical language throughout.
Secure (3-4): Correct links between cardiovascular function and swimming endurance. Partial counterargument or no clear judgement.
Developing (2): Basic points about heart rate or oxygen delivery without developed reasoning.
Emerging (1): Vague reference to heart and exercise.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the formula for cardiac output?
flashcard_questions.a: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate.
The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle with each heartbeat (in ml).

flashcard_questions.q: Which valve sits between the left atrium and left ventricle?
Which valve sits between the right atrium and right ventricle?
Which vessel carries deoxygenated blood from the heart to the lungs?
Which vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
Why are capillaries the site of oxygen delivery to muscles?
flashcard_questions.a: Their single-cell-thick walls allow oxygen to diffuse directly into muscle fibres.
Redistribution of blood to working muscles via vasoconstriction and vasodilation.

flashcard_questions.q: What prevents blood flowing backwards in veins?
What is the role of the septum in the heart?
flashcard_questions.a: Divides left and right sides, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mixing.

flashcard_questions.q: What does resting cardiac output increase to during maximal exercise?
flashcard_questions.a: From ~5 L/min at rest to over 20 L/min during maximal exercise.

glossary_terms.definition: The muscular wall dividing the left and right sides of the heart, preventing oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing.
Either of the two upper chambers of the heart that receive blood returning to the heart.
Either of the two lower, thick-walled chambers of the heart that pump blood out to the lungs or body.
The valve between the right atrium and right ventricle, with three flaps, that prevents backflow of blood.
The valve between the left atrium and left ventricle, with two flaps, that prevents backflow of blood.
Valves located at the exits of the right and left ventricles that prevent blood flowing back into the heart from the pulmonary artery and aorta.
The volume of blood ejected by the heart per minute, calculated as stroke volume multiplied by heart rate.
The volume of blood ejected from the left ventricle with each heartbeat, measured in millilitres.
The number of times the heart beats per minute.
Thick-walled, elastic blood vessels that carry oxygenated blood away from the heart under high pressure.
Tiny, single-cell-walled blood vessels where the exchange of oxygen, carbon dioxide and nutrients between blood and tissues takes place.
Thin-walled blood vessels that carry deoxygenated blood back to the heart, containing valves to prevent backflow.
The redistribution of blood flow away from non-essential organs towards working muscles during exercise, controlled by vasoconstriction and vasodilation.
